title: Glass Tricks
description: Prince Rupert's hammer-proof drops, a plate that bounced, and a glass shelved until the iPhone

concepts.title: Prince Rupert's Drops: Tough Head, Fatal Tail
concepts.contentHtml:
Drip a blob of red-hot glass into a bucket of cold water and it freezes into a little glass tadpole: a round head and a long, threadlike tail. Hit the head with a hammer and it survives. Snap the tail with your fingers and the whole drop bursts into powder with a sharp pop.1 The drops are named after Prince Rupert of the Rhine, who helped get them to King Charles II, and in 1661 the king handed them to the new Royal Society to work out what was going on.2

Robert Hooke took up the puzzle in his 1665 book Micrographia. He coated a drop in fish glue so the pieces stayed in place when he snapped the tail, letting him study the cracks. His explanation was close to the mark: the outside, touching the water, set hard at once, while the inside, insulated by that hard shell, cooled more slowly.3

That slow inner cooling is the trick. The hot core shrinks as it cools, but the skin is already rigid, so the core ends up tugging inward on it. The result is a surface squeezed in compression around a core stretched in tension. Cracks grow only where glass is being pulled apart, so a squeezed surface shrugs off blows. In 2016 a team from Estonia, the United States and Britain measured the squeeze with polarized light: 400–700 megapascals at the surface, as strong as some grades of steel.4 The tail is the weak point. It is thin enough to snap, and once a crack reaches the stretched core, the stored energy drives it through the whole drop. In 1994, high-speed photography at nearly a million frames per second caught cracks racing from tail to head at more than 4,000 mph.5

concepts.title: The Plate That Bounced
concepts.contentHtml:
Sometime in 1952 or 1953 (accounts differ),1 Corning chemist Donald Stookey put a disc of an experimental glass called Fotoform into a furnace set at 600°C. The furnace malfunctioned and climbed to 900°C. Expecting a molten mess, he found an opaque, milky-white disc that had kept its shape. As he lifted it out, his tongs slipped and it fell to the floor, where it bounced, unbroken, clanging like a piece of steel.2

The heat had turned glass into a ceramic. Ordinary glass is a frozen liquid: its atoms are jumbled with no crystal order, which is why it softens and slumps when hot. Fotoform was made to grow tiny crystals in patches exposed to light and then warmed. Pushed 300 degrees hotter than planned, crystals had taken over the whole disc, leaving almost no glass to melt. The new material, later called Fotoceram, was mostly crystals of lithium disilicate and stronger than the glass it started as.3

Stookey spent years turning the accident into a method. The metal seeds behind his light-sensitive glasses did not work in most other glasses, so he tried titania, which seeded crystals throughout and barely let the shapes sag. By the late 1950s this had produced missile nose cones and CorningWare, cookware made of a crystal, beta-spodumene, that hardly expands when heated.4 A dish that hardly expands is hard to crack by sudden heating or cooling. CorningWare went on sale in 1958, and glass-ceramics suited nose cones because they are hard, strong, heat-resistant and transparent to radar.5

concepts.title: Muscle Glass: Shelved in 1971, Called Back for the iPhone
concepts.contentHtml:
Flush with Pyroceram's success, Corning launched Project Muscle, a big push to find other ways of strengthening glass. Its scientists found that glass with added aluminum oxide, soaked in a bath of hot potassium salt, became remarkably tough. They threw strengthened tumblers off their nine-story building and pelted the glass with frozen chickens. It could take 100,000 pounds per square inch, against about 7,000 for normal glass, and in 1962 Corning began selling it as Chemcor for phone booths, prison windows and eyeglasses.1

Hardly anyone wanted it. Carmakers saw little reason to pay more when their laminated windshields worked fine, and after pitches to Ford and others failed, Corning shut the project down and shelved Chemcor in 1971.2

Then phones went glass. In 2005, after Motorola's Razr V3 flip phone used a glass screen instead of plastic, Corning set a small team to see whether the old Chemcor glass could be revived, under the code name Gorilla Glass. In February 2007 Steve Jobs called: Apple wanted huge amounts of 1.3-millimeter chemically strengthened glass, something nobody had ever made.3 Corning reworked the recipe and made it at its plant in Harrodsburg, Kentucky, which has made glass for the iPhone ever since the first one in 2007.4

The strengthening is a swap of atoms. The glass contains sodium, and in the hot potassium bath sodium ions drift out of the surface while potassium ions move in to take their place. Potassium ions are bigger, so they are crammed into spaces sized for sodium, like parking SUVs in bays built for small cars. As the glass cools, the crowded surface is left in compression: the same armor that guards the head of a Prince Rupert's drop, made by chemistry instead of sudden cooling.5

title: Toys From the War Effort
description: Silly Putty from a failed rubber, the Slinky from a ship spring, and Velcro from burrs on a dog

concepts.title: Silly Putty: The Rubber That Failed
concepts.contentHtml:
The Second World War brought a shortage of natural rubber, and chemists hunted for substitutes. In 1943, so the official story goes, James Wright, an engineer at General Electric's laboratories in New Haven, added boric acid to silicone oil and got a goo that bounced when he threw it on the floor and stretched further than natural rubber.1 The story has a rival. Earl Warrick and Rob Roy McGregor, working for Dow Corning at the Mellon Institute in Pittsburgh, made a "bouncing putty" of their own and applied for a patent on March 30, 1943, which may give them the better claim.2

Nobody could find a use for it. In 1945 GE sent samples to engineers around the world, with no luck. Then, in one version of the story, an out-of-work advertising man named Peter Hodgson saw the putty at a party in 1949, bought the rights, renamed it Silly Putty and sold it in plastic eggs. After a 1950 piece in The New Yorker, orders came in for a quarter of a million eggs in just over three days.3 In 1968 the Apollo 8 astronauts took some on their flight around the Moon, to relieve stress and to stick tools to the spacecraft's walls.4

The odd behavior comes from its chemistry. Silly Putty is a borosilicone: long silicone chains tied together by boron cross-links. At any instant the links hold the chains in a rubbery network, so a ball bounces. But each link is temporary, breaking and re-forming with new partners, so given time the network rearranges and the putty flows like a very thick liquid. Solid or liquid depends on how fast you ask: a bounce is over before the links can let go, while a lump left on a shelf slowly sags into a puddle.5

concepts.title: The Slinky: A Spring That Walks and a Bottom That Waits
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1943 Richard James, a mechanical engineer in Philadelphia, was working on springs to keep delicate instruments steady aboard ships in rough seas. He knocked one off a shelf, and instead of landing in a heap it "stepped" in a series of arcs, from the shelf to a stack of books to a tabletop to the floor, where it re-coiled itself and stood upright.1 He spent two years testing metals and proportions. His wife, Betty, leafed through a dictionary for a name and chose "slinky," meaning graceful in movement.2 On the evening of November 27, 1945, he demonstrated it at Gimbels department store in Philadelphia, and all 400 he had, at $1 each, sold out in 90 minutes.3

A Slinky has a second trick. Hold one by its top end, let it hang and stretch under its own weight, then let go. The top plunges, but the bottom stays exactly where it was, hanging in midair, until the coils collapsing from above crash into it, roughly 0.3 seconds later for a real Slinky.4

Nothing is defying gravity. Before you let go, each coil is in balance: gravity pulls it down and the stretched coils above pull it up. Letting go removes the pull only at the very top. That news has to travel down the spring as a wave, coil by coil, and until it arrives the bottom coils feel exactly the same forces as before, so they stay put. The Slinky as a whole still obeys the usual rule: its center of mass falls with the ordinary acceleration of gravity from the instant you let go.5

concepts.title: Velcro: Burrs on the Dog
concepts.contentHtml:
Not every invention of the war years came from the war. In 1941, in neutral Switzerland, the engineer George de Mestral came back from a walk in the woods with his dog and found his woolen socks, his jacket and the dog's fur covered in burdock burrs.1 He put one under his microscope and saw that it was covered in tiny hooks that caught on the loops of fabric and in animal hair: the plant's way of getting its seeds carried far and wide.2

Copying the burr took years. Few people took the idea seriously, but with help from a weaver in Lyon and a loom-maker in Basel he found that nylon, sewn under infrared light, formed tough hooks. Weaving some 300 hooks and loops per square inch onto tape made progress slow, and the fastener was patented in 1955 under the name Velcro, from the French velours (velvet) and crochet (hook).3 His United States patent, filed in 1952 after a Swiss application in 1951, shows the trick: loop nylon thread over a heated bar so it sets in shape, then cut each loop on one side, leaving a hook.4

A hook-and-loop fastener holds because thousands of hooks share the load, so pulling the strips straight apart is hard. Peeling is easy because it frees only the row of hooks at the edge at any moment, and those small releases make the familiar rasp. Velcro is often credited to the space program, but it is not a NASA invention.5

title: Lost Secrets and Legends
description: Starlite's blowtorched egg, Rome's unbreakable glass, and a priest's silk bulletproof vest

concepts.title: Starlite and the Egg That Wouldn't Cook
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1990 the BBC science show Tomorrow's World pitted two eggs against a blowtorch. The bare egg cracked almost at once. The other wore a coat of a material called Starlite. Minutes later the presenter switched off the flame, held the egg in his palm and cracked it into a bowl. It was still raw.1

Its inventor, Maurice Ward, was a hairdresser with no training in chemistry or materials science, though he liked experimenting with new hair colors. Starlite, named by his granddaughter, was a white powder mixed with ordinary PVA glue.2

Then the claims grew. According to Ward, Starlite went on to survive a battery of tests at Britain's Atomic Weapons Establishment, including a nuclear flash equal to 75 Hiroshima bombs at up to 10,000°C. Investors, and reportedly even NASA, came calling, but Ward refused to sign any confidentiality agreement, afraid that companies would copy his formula.3 He died in 2011, aged 78, still keeping the recipe secret, though some reports say he passed it to his family.4

So what was it? Ward's daughters later took a sample to the materials scientist Mark Miodownik at University College London. Under heat, he explained, the coating chars into a very light, expanding foam of carbon, a material with a very high melting point. Coatings that swell like this are called intumescent, and the first was patented in 1948. Even the egg trick proves less than it seems: one tester found that almost any white paste keeps an egg from cooking for three minutes. The skeptic Brian Dunning's verdict: a fine coating, perhaps, but by no means a revolutionary one.5

concepts.title: Rome's Unbreakable Glass
concepts.contentHtml:
In Petronius's Satyricon, a character at a dinner party tells of a craftsman who brought the emperor a glass vial that could not be broken. He threw it on the floor. It came up dented, like a brass bowl, and he beat the dent out with a little hammer from his tunic. The emperor asked whether anyone else knew how to make this glass. When the man said no, the emperor had his head cut off, because if the secret got out, gold would be worth no more than dirt.1

Two other Roman writers tell versions of the tale. Pliny the Elder, in his Natural History, mentions a flexible glass invented in the reign of Tiberius.2 He says the glassmaker's whole workshop was destroyed so that copper, silver and gold would not lose their value, but he plainly doubted it, adding that the story was told more often than it was reliable. Cassius Dio makes the craftsman an architect, exiled by a jealous Tiberius, who threw a glass vessel on the floor and repaired the damage with his bare hands. Not surprisingly, no example of Roman vitrum flexile, flexible glass, is known to exist.3

Bendable glass does exist now, and the secret is thinness, not a lost recipe. In 2012 Corning launched Willow Glass, 100 microns thick, about the thickness of a sheet of copy paper.4 Everyday glass shatters when bent because a thick sheet puts extreme tension on the outer face of the curve. Make it thin enough and the strain on that face becomes so low that the glass curves instead of breaking. The glass layer in one new folding phone is reportedly less than 30 micrometers thick, much finer than a human hair.5

concepts.title: The Priest in the Silk Vest
concepts.contentHtml:
On March 16, 1897, in a Chicago square, a marksman walked eight paces, raised his revolver and fired at the chest of a Catholic priest, the Reverend Casimir Zeglen. Zeglen fell, then got back to his feet, raised his hands and told the cheering crowd he was unharmed. He had hired the marksman himself to test his silk armor, and his vests would later be sold around the world, including to heads of state.1 His vest was hand-sewn from silk, linen and wool and was half an inch thick. Chicago had reason to care: its former mayor, Carter Harrison Sr., had been murdered at his home four years earlier.2

The trick was in the layering. Zeglen's patents, granted on March 2, 1897, describe layers of strong cords, preferably silk, with the strands in each layer lying parallel and each layer laid crosswise to the next, backed with hair or wool and stitched together. The fabric was meant to stop projectiles by cushioning and absorbing their impact while staying light and flexible enough to wear as clothing.3

Its most famous possible owner was Archduke Franz Ferdinand, whose assassination led directly to the First World War. Britain's Royal Armouries museum says he owned a Zeglen vest but did not wear it on the day he was shot.4 Newspapers at the time claimed the opposite: that he was wearing it, and that the assassin, tipped off by an insider, aimed at his neck instead. In 2014 the Royal Armouries had replica vests made to Zeglen's original patent and tested them with ammunition and a pistol like the 1910 Browning the assassin used. Just as Zeglen had claimed, the silk could stop bullets. But the fatal shot hit the Archduke in the neck, so a vest might not have saved him anyway.5

title: Miracle Materials That Weren't
description: LK-99's half-floating flake, Ranga Dias's retracted superconductors, lost metallic hydrogen

concepts.title: LK-99's Summer of Hype
concepts.contentHtml:
On July 22, 2023, three researchers posted a paper online titled "The First Room-Temperature Ambient-Pressure Superconductor." Their material, LK-99, was a modified lead apatite, and they said it superconducted up to at least 127°C, hotter than boiling water, at ordinary pressure, showing zero resistance and the Meissner effect.1

The Meissner effect was the claim anyone could watch: a superconductor placed on a magnet levitates. In a video meant to show LK-99 doing it, the flake never fully left the magnet. Physicists were unconvinced, pointing out that a sample which is only partly magnetic can behave the same way.2

Labs raced to make LK-99, and the mystery unraveled within weeks. On August 9 the chemist Prashant Jain pointed out that the copper-doped material, as made, contains a significant fraction of copper(I) sulfide. At 104°C that compound changes from an ordered structure to a superionic one, and its electrical resistance changes sharply, which should line up with the transitions reported for LK-99.3 Another team grew pure single crystals of LK-99. They were transparent and highly insulating, with only a small ferromagnetic signal, and the team ruled out superconductivity.4

In December 2023, after four months of checking replication experiments in Korea and abroad, the Korean Society of Superconductivity and Cryogenics concluded there was "no evidence at all" that LK-99 is a room-temperature, ambient-pressure superconductor. The papers' data, it said, had failed to show zero resistance or the repulsion of magnetic fields.5

concepts.title: Retracted: Ranga Dias's Superconductors
concepts.contentHtml:
In 2020 the journal Nature published what looked like a landmark. Ranga Dias's group reported that a carbonaceous sulfur hydride, squeezed in a diamond anvil cell to 267 gigapascals, became a superconductor at 287.7 kelvin, about 15°C: room temperature, if only under crushing pressure.1

Questions were raised about how the data had been processed, and Nature's editors retracted the paper. Their notice says the background subtractions behind its key magnetic plots used "a non-standard, user-defined procedure" the paper did not describe, undermining confidence in that data. The authors maintained that their raw data supported the claim, and all of them disagreed with the retraction.2

In March 2023 the lab published a second Nature paper, claiming superconductivity near room temperature and pressure in a nitrogen-doped lutetium hydride. It too was retracted, this time at the request of eight of its own co-authors, who said it did not accurately reflect the materials, measurements or data processing. The journal also judged separate concerns about its resistance data credible, substantial and unresolved. Dias did not say whether he agreed.3

In March 2024 the University of Rochester, where Dias worked, said an investigation had found he "engaged in research misconduct." Dias blamed "an individual's opinion and apparent errors in understanding the data" and accused the university of predetermining the outcome.4 The committee's report upheld all 15 allegations about the papers and one about a grant proposal, finding that he "engaged in falsification, fabrication, and/or plagiarism of data, images, and text." It stressed that its job was not to judge whether the physics was right, only whether the allegations met the definition of research misconduct.5

concepts.title: Metallic Hydrogen and the Vanished Sample
concepts.contentHtml:
One autumn day in 2016, the Harvard physicist Isaac Silvera got a phone call from his postdoc, Ranga Dias: "It's shining!" The "it" was a speck of solid hydrogen 10 micrometers across in a diamond anvil cell. As Dias raised the pressure, it had gone from transparent to black and then to reflective, the expected signature of a metal, at an estimated 495 gigapascals. Physicists had chased metallic hydrogen since Eugene Wigner and Hillard Huntington predicted it in 1935, and many in the field had serious reservations about this sighting.1

Part of the prize is cosmic. Scientists think that deep inside Jupiter, perhaps halfway to the center, the pressure is so great that electrons are squeezed off the hydrogen atoms and the liquid conducts electricity like a metal. The spinning of that liquid metallic hydrogen is thought to act as a dynamo, generating the planet's powerful magnetic field.2

Silvera and Dias published in Science in late January 2017. Then they lost the sample. Before shipping it to Argonne National Laboratory, they shone a laser into the cell to check the pressure, with less power than in a test months earlier, and the diamonds broke instantly. "We could hear it click," Silvera said. "It's not mysterious, it's the way experiments end."3

Whether that speck was ever metallic hydrogen is still disputed. In 2024 the University of Rochester committee investigating Dias's later work wrote that the hydrogen paper's results "have not been accepted by nearly all expert peers."4 The hunt goes on. In 2020 another team reported a sudden drop in hydrogen's band gap near 425 gigapascals, which they called most probably the start of the metallic state, while noting that the various earlier claims of metallic hydrogen remain unconfirmed.5
